summary.text: According to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(4\), subtract \(0,9,18\), or \(27\); the remainder is a nonnegative multiple \(4q\), which is expressed as a sum of distinct terms \(4\cdot 2^i\) using the binary expansion of \(q\). These terms are nonsquarefree because they are divisible by \(4\), while the optional subtracted term is divisible by \(9\), yielding a partition into distinct nonsquarefree parts.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
U_n=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
\]
By definition, \(a(n)\) is the number of finite subsets \(P\subseteq U_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{x\in P}x=n
\quad\text{and}\quad
\text{every }x\in P\text{ is not squarefree}.
\]
Because a subset has no repeated elements, such a set is exactly a partition of \(n\) into distinct nonsquarefree parts. We prove that for every \(n>23\), at least one such set \(P\) exists.

We first construct distinct nonsquarefree parts whose sum is any prescribed multiple of \(4\).

For each nonnegative integer \(m\), define a finite set \(B(m)\) recursively as follows. Set
\[
B(0)=\varnothing.
\]
For \(m>0\), put \(q=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\), and let
\[
2B(q)=\{2x:x\in B(q)\}.
\]
Then define
\[
B(m)=
\begin{cases}
2B(q),&m\text{ even},\\
\{4\}\cup 2B(q),&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(B(m)\) consists of selected members of \(\{4,8,16,32,\ldots\}\), with the selections corresponding to the binary digits of \(m\). The recursive description alone will suffice.

We establish three properties of \(B(m)\):

1. every member of \(B(m)\) is divisible by \(4\);
2. every member of \(B(m)\) is positive;
3. the sum of the members of \(B(m)\) is \(4m\).

These follow by strong induction on \(m\). They are immediate for \(m=0\), since \(B(0)\) is empty. Suppose \(m>0\), let \(q=\lfloor m/2\rfloor<m\), and assume the claims for \(B(q)\). Every member of \(2B(q)\) has the form \(2x\), where \(x\) is a positive multiple of \(4\). Hence \(2x\) is again positive and divisible by \(4\). If \(m\) is odd, the only additional member is \(4\), which has the same two properties. This proves the first two assertions.

For the sum assertion, multiplication by \(2\) is injective on the nonnegative integers, so doubling all members does not create repetitions, and
\[
\sum_{y\in 2B(q)}y
 =\sum_{x\in B(q)}2x
 =2\sum_{x\in B(q)}x
 =2(4q)=8q.
\]
If \(m\) is even, then \(m=2q\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{y\in B(m)}y=8q=4m.
\]
If \(m\) is odd, then \(m=2q+1\). In this case \(4\notin 2B(q)\): indeed, every element of \(B(q)\) is divisible by \(4\), so every element of \(2B(q)\) is divisible by \(8\), whereas \(4\) is not. Thus adjoining \(4\) genuinely adds one new member, and
\[
\sum_{y\in B(m)}y=4+8q=4(2q+1)=4m.
\]
This completes the induction.

In particular, all parts in \(B(m)\) are nonsquarefree. Indeed, if \(x\) is divisible by \(4\), then \(2^2=4\mid x\). Since \(2\) is not a unit, the existence of the nontrivial square divisor \(2^2\) shows that \(x\) is not squarefree.

We now construct the desired set for \(n>23\). Define \(P_n\) according to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(4\):
\[
P_n=
\begin{cases}
B(n/4),&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2mm]
\{9\}\cup B((n-9)/4),&n\equiv1\pmod4,\\[2mm]
\{18\}\cup B((n-18)/4),&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2mm]
\{27\}\cup B((n-27)/4),&n\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
All the displayed quotients are nonnegative integers in their respective cases. To see this carefully, \(n>23\) means \(n\ge24\). If \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), the smallest possibility is \(25\), so \(n\ge9\), and \(n-9\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(4\). If \(n\equiv2\pmod4\), the smallest possibility is \(26\), so \(n\ge18\), and \(n-18\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(4\). If \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), the smallest possibility is \(27\), so \(n\ge27\), and \(n-27\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(4\).

We verify separately in the four cases that the sum of the members of \(P_n\) is \(n\).

If \(n\equiv0\pmod4\), write \(n=4q\). Then \(P_n=B(q)\), and the property of \(B\) proved above gives
\[
\sum_{x\in P_n}x=4q=n.
\]

If \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), write \(n=9+4q\), where \(q=(n-9)/4\). Every member of \(B(q)\) is divisible by \(4\), while \(9\) is not, so \(9\notin B(q)\). Therefore the union defining \(P_n\) is disjoint and
\[
\sum_{x\in P_n}x
 =9+\sum_{x\in B(q)}x
 =9+4q=n.
\]

If \(n\equiv2\pmod4\), write \(n=18+4q\), where \(q=(n-18)/4\). Since \(18\) is not divisible by \(4\), it is not in \(B(q)\), and hence
\[
\sum_{x\in P_n}x
 =18+\sum_{x\in B(q)}x
 =18+4q=n.
\]

Finally, if \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), write \(n=27+4q\), where \(q=(n-27)/4\). Again \(27\) is not divisible by \(4\), so \(27\notin B(q)\), and
\[
\sum_{x\in P_n}x
 =27+\sum_{x\in B(q)}x
 =27+4q=n.
\]
Thus in every case \(P_n\) is a finite set of distinct positive integers summing to \(n\).

It remains to verify that every part is nonsquarefree. We already know this for every member coming from a set \(B(q)\), because such a member is divisible by \(2^2=4\). The exceptional parts are also nonsquarefree:
\[
3^2=9\mid9,
\qquad
3^2=9\mid18,
\qquad
3^2=9\mid27.
\]
Since \(3\) is not a unit, each of \(9,18,27\) has a nontrivial square divisor and is therefore not squarefree. Consequently every element of \(P_n\) is nonsquarefree.

For completeness, \(P_n\) really is a subset of \(U_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), as required by the definition of \(a(n)\). We have shown that all its members are positive. If \(x\in P_n\), then all members of \(P_n\) are nonnegative, so one summand cannot exceed their total:
\[
x\le \sum_{y\in P_n}y=n.
\]
Thus \(1\le x\le n\), proving \(P_n\subseteq U_n\).

We have therefore exhibited, for every \(n>23\), a finite subset \(P_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) whose elements are distinct and nonsquarefree and whose sum is \(n\). Hence the collection counted by \(a(n)\) is nonempty. Its cardinality is consequently positive, so
\[
a(n)>0
\]
for every integer \(n>23\), as claimed.
